The company added that MDASH includes enterprise controls such as role-based access controls, tenant isolation, encryption, audit logging and sandboxed execution environments without internet access.Explaining the motivation behind the announcements, Microsoft said,
Article Summary: Microsoft unveils Project Perception and MAI-Cyber-1-Flash. Project Perception is Microsoft's new agentic cybersecurity system. MAI is the company's first AI model built specifically for software vulnerability analysis. Microsoft claims that the new cybersecurity model outperforms Gemini and GPT on vulnerability- detection benchmarks.

Article Title: OpenAI's rogue AI agent that hacked world's biggest repository of AI models also left a ‘cheat code’ that tells hackers ...
Article Text:
AI agents data vulnerability

AI agent hacking Hugging Face went unnoticed for a week



The incident involving OpenAI’s AI agent escaping the sandbox and going on to hack Hugging Face – the world’s largest AI model repository – has escalated AI safety concerns. However, the bigger concerns are related to the detailed instructions it left behind explaining how future AI models can bypass internal safety controls.Citing sources familiar with the investigation, news agency Reuters claimed that the rogue agent penned notes within OpenAI's internal infrastructure outlining how subsequent AI systems could break free from company-imposed constraints. Earlier safety testing on the underlying models had already revealed instances where monitoring systems were mysteriously disconnected.The revelations provide new insight into a multi-day breach that went unnoticed by OpenAI until days after the threat was contained by Hugging Face and reported to the FBI. The report explained that the break-in involved an experimental agent powered by two of OpenAI’s most advanced systems: the cybersecurity-focused GPT-5.6 Sol and an even more powerful, unreleased model.The agent managed to break out of its isolated testing environment before launching an external attack. The report also says that the attack went on for two days: From July 11 to July 13. Hugging Face reported the incident a week later.Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf confirmed that the firm is preparing a public timeline detailing the intrusion, which compromised internal datasets and credentials before being shut down. The company also said that it used an open-source Chinese model to curb the attack as American models’ restrictions ‘failed’ to contain the cyberattack.This was followed by an announcement by OpenAI that it was the company’s agent that hacked the repository. In a formal statement, OpenAI called the event an “unprecedented” moment for AI safety, confirming that it is working with external advisors to review its sandboxing protocols and plans to publish a comprehensive technical report on the breach.
Article Summary: OpenAI’s AI agent escaped the sandbox and went on to hack Hugging Face. The breach went unnoticed by OpenAI until days after the threat was contained. The rogue agent penned notes outlining how subsequent AI systems could break free from company-imposed constraints.

Wall Street rattled by cost-effective rivals

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has pushed back against Wall Street’s anxieties over low-cost Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models, arguing that global trust in American infrastructure and its open ecosystem will keep US tech giants ahead. His comments come at a time when there is an industry-wide debate on open-source AI models versus proprietary models. Speaking with CNN, Nadella addressed concerns surrounding Chinese AI models, such as Moonshot AI’s recently released Kimi K3, which offer advanced coding and reasoning capabilities at a fraction of the cost of US alternatives.When asked if cheaper Chinese technologies hold a competitive edge, Nadella emphasised that American hyperscalers still form the backbone of global AI deployment.Nadella said.Nadella highlighted that since many Chinese developers release open-weight models, Western companies can run, test, monitor and post-train those systems on their own secure platforms. He noted that critics worrying about price competition are missing the broader picture of how the US built its technological dominance in the first place.Nadella explained, adding,Nadella’s comments come during a heightened investor sensitivity over massive US AI spending. Microsoft holds a roughly 27% stake in OpenAI 's for-profit public benefit arm, investing billions to maintain top-tier model performance.However, Chinese AI labs have repeatedly disrupted market expectations. For example, last year, the launch of DeepSeek sparked a $1 trillion tech stock sell-off, proving China could develop highly capable models at vastly lower costs. Similarly, in July, Chinese company Moonshot AI released Kimi K3. The AI model drew interest for matching the reasoning and coding benchmarks of Western models offered by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI.

What upset US Federal Agents



GrapheneOS can also get smartphone users in trouble in Europe

What cybersecurity researchers say



A Federal case in Atlanta has raised questions about whether the use of privacy-focused mobile software can be treated as evidence of criminal intent, after prosecutors accused a man of wiping his phone to prevent authorities from accessing its contents. The US Department of Justice is prosecuting Atlanta resident Samuel Tunick under a federal law that makes it a crime to destroy property to prevent its seizure, The Guardian reported. First reported by The Guardian, the case centres on GrapheneOS, a custom Android operating system that runs in place of the software on most modern Google Pixel devices. These include the ability to erase a device by entering a designated passcode. The incident occurred at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on January 24, after Tunick returned from the Dominican Republic. Tunick’s attorneys confirmed GrapheneOS was running on his phone.Agents repeatedly asked Tunick to unlock his phone and warned that it would be seized if he refused. After he eventually provided a passcode, “the screen went blank, flashed several times, and the phone appeared to restart,” according to the defence motion.Data stored on the device was subsequently lost. Prosecutors allege that the wipe was a deliberate attempt to destroy potential evidence. Tunick’s lawyers maintain that the underlying search violated his constitutional rights. The GrapheneOS has a feature that allows the device owner to set a passcode that deliberately wipes the contents of that device if entered instead of the user’s unlock passcode.According to court testimony cited by The Guardian, federal agents had circulated his name and photograph internally over alleged links to the movement opposing Atlanta’s police training centre, commonly known as Cop City. Tunick was reportedly taken to a secondary screening area and questioned by several agents. A defence filing alleges that questions about child sexual abuse material were used as a pretext to investigate his association with the protest movement. Tunick's lawyers are seeking to have the case dismissed, arguing that US Customs and Border Protection agents unlawfully seized his phone when he returned to the country last year. They contend that any evidence arising from the incident, including the alleged deletion of the phone’s data, should be suppressed.While GrapheneOS supporters argue that its features are legitimate safeguards against surveillance and data theft, authorities in parts of Europe too reportedly treat the operating system’s use as suspicious. In Catalonia, Spain, police have reportedly been profiling people with Google Pixel phones, assuming they have GrapheneOS installed and are drug dealers or gang members.Following the report on Samuel Tunick's arrest, GrapheneOS published a lengthy thread explaining that its security model is designed to prevent unauthorised data extraction rather than rely on features that erase phone data. It went ion to stress that the OS is completely legal. "GrapheneOS is completely legal. We have no obligation to weaken any of the security protections it provides. Creating and using GrapheneOS is strongly protected by the US constitution. Laws attempting to make it illegal or require weakening the security would be unconstitutional," reads a post from GrapheneOS. On data erading, it adds, "There's no way to bypass a strong encryption passphrase once data is at rest. A typical weak PIN or password depends on the secure element limiting the number of attempts. Secure element only accepts firmware updates after Owner authenticates to protect against state coercion. By default, GrapheneOS devices automatically return to Before First Unlock state if they aren't unlocked within 18 hours of being locked. Users can set it as low as 10 minutes. GrapheneOS has strong generic exploit protections and specialized defenses against physical attacks."Cybersecurity experts told the publication that the prosecution’s legal strategy appeared unprecedented. Christophe Boutry, a cybersecurity and surveillance expert, told The Guardian, “It’s concerning – and sends the message that [GrapheneOS] is criminal by default.”
Article Summary: Atlanta resident Samuel Tunick is accused of wiping his phone to prevent authorities from accessing its contents. He is being prosecuted under a federal law that makes it a crime to destroy property to prevent its seizure. The case centres on GrapheneOS, a custom Android operating system that runs in place of the software on most modern Google Pixel devices.
